content: The term vitamer refers to the various chemical compounds that exhibit the biological activity of a specific vitamin. Vitamins are often not single chemical entities; instead, each vitamin, defined by its biological function rather than its chemical structure, is represented by a group of compounds that all demonstrate the same vitamin activity. The biological activity of multiple vitamers is typically influenced by the body's limited ability to convert one vitamer into another or to transform several vitamers into the same enzymatic cofactor(s). This limitation exists even though, by definition, the body cannot synthesize an optimal amount of a vitamin from basic dietary components without the presence of at least one vitamer molecule as a precursor. Not all vitamers have identical vitamin potency per unit of mass. This variation arises from differences in the absorption and interconversion of the various vitamers of a given vitamin. Similarly, the toxicity of vitamers can differ depending on the specific molecule, as is observed with vitamin E. A group of related chemical compounds may sometimes (but not always) be categorized under a generic descriptor, such as vitamin A, which includes compounds like retinal, retinol, and various carotenoids. Examples of vitamers include cyanocobalamin, hydroxocobalamin, methylcobalamin, and 5-deoxyadenosylcobalamin (also known as adenosylcobalamin or AdoB-12), all of which are vitamers of vitamin B-12 and share B-12 activity. Another example is that both niacinamide and nicotinic acid (niacin) exhibit vitamin B-3 activity. Some vitamins have not been assigned specific alphabetic generic descriptors by naming authorities and are instead known by names such as biotin and folate. These are B vitamins but lack a designated B number. However, even these vitamins consist of multiple active vitamers that function in both dietary sources and cellular processes.
